description: Platform engineering for a cloud/Kubernetes platform architect: GitOps (Argo CD, Flux), Terraform/Ansible/Crossplane, Helm, operators, internal developer platforms, policy-as-code, supply-chain security, and fleet/multi-tenancy design.

notes.text: OpenGitOps principles: desired state is {{c1::declarative}}; it is {{c2::versioned and immutable}} (full history); it is {{c3::pulled automatically}} by agents from the source; it is {{c4::continuously reconciled}} against the actual state.

notes.front: Push vs pull deployment: where do the cluster credentials live?
notes.back:
Push: the CI pipeline holds cluster credentials and applies changes.
Pull: an in-cluster agent pulls from Git/OCI; credentials never leave the cluster, it only needs read access to the source.
notes.analogy: Push hands a courier the keys to your house; pull means you collect parcels yourself, so nobody else holds a key.
notes.extra: Bonus of pull: the agent keeps correcting drift continuously.

notes.front: Why is "manifests in Git + kubectl apply from CI" not GitOps?
notes.back: Nothing reconciles continuously, so drift from manual changes is never detected or corrected. It is push-based continuous delivery (CD).
notes.analogy: A thermostat keeps measuring and correcting the temperature; a CI apply sets the heater once and walks away.

notes.front: GitOps secrets: encrypted-in-Git vs reference-in-Git — examples of each?
notes.back:
Encrypted in Git: Sealed Secrets, SOPS.
Reference in Git: External Secrets Operator, Secrets Store Container Storage Interface (CSI) driver — Git holds only a pointer to Vault / cloud key management service (KMS).
notes.analogy: Encrypted-in-Git is a locked safe kept in the repo; reference-in-Git is a claim ticket pointing to a safe kept elsewhere.

notes.front: GitOps environment promotion: why prefer directory-per-environment over branch-per-environment?
notes.back: Env differences are visible as diffs on one branch; long-lived env branches drift apart through cherry-picks and merges.

notes.front: State the four OpenGitOps principles and what each one buys you.
notes.back:
Declarative: you describe the end state, not steps.
Versioned and immutable: full history for audit and rollback.
Pulled automatically: agents fetch it, so no external push credentials.
Continuously reconciled: drift gets corrected.

notes.front: A teammate hotfixes a live Deployment with kubectl edit. What happens under GitOps with continuous reconciliation, versus under continuous integration (CI) pipeline push?
notes.back:
GitOps: the agent detects the drift and reverts it (or flags it as out of sync).
CI push: nothing notices; the hotfix lives on until the next pipeline run overwrites it.

notes.front: Why does the pull model shrink the blast radius of a compromised continuous integration (CI) system?
notes.back: CI holds no cluster credentials, so at worst it can change Git, where review and audit apply. In push-based continuous delivery, a hijacked pipeline can act directly on the cluster.

notes.text: Argo CD components: {{c1::argocd-repo-server}} clones repos and renders manifests (Helm/Kustomize/plugins); {{c2::argocd-application-controller}} compares live vs desired state and syncs; {{c3::argocd-server}} serves the API and UI.
notes.extra: Also: Redis (cache), Dex (SSO), ApplicationSet controller, notifications controller.

notes.front: Key fields of an Argo CD Application spec?
notes.back: project, source/sources (repoURL, targetRevision, path or chart), destination (cluster + namespace), syncPolicy.

notes.front: What does an Argo CD AppProject restrict?
notes.back: Allowed source repos, destination clusters/namespaces, and allowed/denied resource kinds (cluster-scoped and namespaced); it also carries project roles and sync windows.
notes.extra: Tenancy pattern: one AppProject per tenant, single sign-on (SSO) groups mapped to project roles, cluster-scoped kinds (e.g. ClusterRole) denied → tenants self-serve within guardrails.

notes.front: Argo CD: sync status vs health status?
notes.back:
Sync: does live state match Git (Synced / OutOfSync)?
Health: is the app actually working (Healthy, Progressing, Degraded, Missing...)?
notes.analogy: Sync asks "is the furniture where the floor plan says?"; health asks "do the lights and water actually work?"
notes.extra: Health comes from built-in or custom Lua health checks.

notes.text: Argo CD automated sync: prune: true {{c1::deletes resources removed from Git}}; selfHeal: true {{c2::reverts manual live changes without a new commit}}.
notes.extra: Pitfall: both are off by default, even when automated sync is enabled.

notes.front: Argo CD sync phases and sync waves: how do they order resources?
notes.back: Phases run PreSync → Sync → PostSync (SyncFail on failure). Within a phase, argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave orders resources (lowest first, may be negative); Argo waits for health between waves.
notes.analogy: A stage crew: set up (PreSync), perform (Sync), clean up (PostSync); waves are the order crews go on stage, each waiting until the previous one is ready.

notes.front: How are Argo CD hooks declared?
notes.back: argocd.argoproj.io/hook: PreSync|Sync|PostSync|SyncFail|Skip plus argocd.argoproj.io/hook-delete-policy (HookSucceeded, HookFailed, BeforeHookCreation).
notes.extra: Helm hook annotations are mapped to Argo hooks.

notes.front: Is a Helm chart deployed by Argo CD a real Helm release?
notes.back: No. Argo renders it with helm template and applies the manifests itself: helm ls shows nothing, lookup returns empty, Argo owns the lifecycle.

notes.front: What is the Argo CD App of Apps pattern?
notes.back: A parent Application whose source contains Application manifests, bootstrapping a whole set of child apps from one entry point.

notes.text: ApplicationSet generators: List = {{c1::fixed items}}; Cluster = {{c2::registered clusters, filtered by labels}}; Git = {{c3::directories or files in a repo}}; Matrix / Merge = {{c4::combine the output of other generators}}.
notes.extra: Also: source control management (SCM) Provider, Pull Request, Cluster Decision Resource, Plugin.

notes.front: ApplicationSet for "deploy add-ons to every cluster labelled env=prod"?
notes.back: A Cluster generator with selector.matchLabels: {env: prod}, templating the cluster name/server into the Application; often combined (Matrix) with a Git directory generator.

notes.front: Why are ApplicationSets the backbone of multi-cluster GitOps?
notes.back: They generate one Application per target cluster, so registering and labelling a new cluster is enough for the golden stack and tenant apps to roll onto it.
notes.extra: Flux equivalent: per-cluster bootstrap from a shared repo layout (clusters/<name>/ overlays).

notes.front: How do multi-source Applications help with Helm charts?
notes.back: spec.sources lets a chart from a Helm/OCI repo take values files from a separate Git repo via a ref source, e.g. valueFiles: [$values/envs/prod.yaml].

notes.front: How do you stop Argo CD flagging fields mutated by other controllers (e.g. HPA-managed replicas)?
notes.back: ignoreDifferences (jsonPointers, jqPathExpressions or managedFieldsManagers) plus sync option RespectIgnoreDifferences=true so syncs don't overwrite them.

notes.text: Argo CD sync options: {{c1::CreateNamespace=true}} creates the destination namespace; {{c2::ServerSideApply=true}} applies via server-side apply (e.g. custom resource definitions (CRDs) too large for the last-applied annotation); {{c3::PruneLast=true}} prunes only after everything else has synced.

notes.front: How does Argo CD track which resources belong to an app, and what changed in 3.0?
notes.back: Via a tracking method: the argocd.argoproj.io/tracking-id annotation (default since 3.0) or the app.kubernetes.io/instance label (old default, clashes with Helm's use of that label).

notes.front: How is a remote cluster registered in Argo CD?
notes.back: argocd cluster add creates a ServiceAccount + RBAC in the target and stores its credentials as a Secret labelled argocd.argoproj.io/secret-type: cluster in the Argo namespace.
notes.extra: That Secret can also be declared directly (GitOps-managed cluster registration).

notes.front: Argo CD topology: hub-and-spoke vs instance-per-cluster trade-off?
notes.back:
Hub: single pane of glass and central RBAC, but needs network access + credentials for every cluster (blast radius, scale bottleneck).
Per-cluster: isolation and pull-only networking, but N instances to run.
notes.analogy: One central air-traffic tower for many airports vs a tower at every airport.

notes.front: How often does Argo CD poll Git, and how do you make it react immediately?
notes.back: About every 3 minutes (timeout.reconciliation = 180s plus jitter). Configure Git provider webhooks to /api/webhook for immediate refresh.

notes.front: Argo CD: refresh vs hard refresh?
notes.back:
Refresh: re-compare using cached manifests (checks the Git revision).
Hard refresh: invalidates the repo-server manifest cache and re-renders.
notes.analogy: Refresh re-checks the cached printout against the latest version; hard refresh throws the printout away and reprints.

notes.front: How do you scale the Argo CD application controller across many clusters?
notes.back: Run multiple replicas with sharding by cluster (legacy, round-robin or consistent-hashing), and tune --status-processors / --operation-processors.

notes.front: What are Argo CD Config Management Plugins (CMPs)?
notes.back: Custom manifest generators run as sidecars on the repo-server (a ConfigManagementPlugin in plugin.yaml), e.g. for cdk8s, Jsonnet variants, envsubst.

notes.front: Where is Argo CD RBAC configured?
notes.back: In argocd-rbac-cm policy.csv (Casbin): p, role:x, applications, sync, proj/*, allow and g, sso-group, role:x; plus AppProject roles.

notes.front: Why do the Argo CD docs discourage manifest-injecting secret plugins (e.g. argocd-vault-plugin)?
notes.back: The secrets end up in rendered manifests cached in Redis/repo-server and visible to anyone who can view the app's manifests. Prefer operators that create Secrets in-cluster (External Secrets, Sealed Secrets).

notes.front: What is Argo Rollouts?
notes.back: A separate controller with a Rollout custom resource definition (CRD) for blue-green and canary delivery: traffic shaping (Istio, NGINX, Gateway API...) plus automated analysis (AnalysisTemplates against Prometheus etc.).

notes.front: In Argo CD with automated sync enabled but selfHeal off, what happens when someone edits a live resource by hand?
notes.back: The app shows OutOfSync, but the manual change stays until the next Git commit or a manual sync. Only selfHeal: true reverts live drift on its own.

notes.front: In Argo CD with prune off, what happens when you delete a manifest from Git?
notes.back: The resource stays in the cluster. The app reports the leftover as needing pruning, so the orphan keeps running until pruned manually or prune: true is set.

notes.front: How do App of Apps and ApplicationSet differ in how child Applications come into existence?
notes.back:
App of Apps: you commit each child Application manifest to Git by hand.
ApplicationSet: a template plus generators produces the Applications automatically from data (clusters, directories, lists).

notes.front: A custom resource and its custom resource definition (CRD) are in the same Argo CD sync. How do you make sure the CRD is applied first?
notes.back: Give the CRD a lower argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave than the custom resource. Argo applies waves in ascending order and waits for health between them.

notes.front: What can a team do from the Argo CD default project that an AppProject restriction would stop?
notes.back: The default project allows any source repo, destination cluster and namespace, and resource kind. A restricted AppProject confines a team to its own repos, namespaces and kinds, which is what makes shared Argo CD multi-tenant.

notes.text: Flux controllers: {{c1::source-controller}} fetches Git/OCI/Helm/Bucket sources into artifacts; {{c2::kustomize-controller}} applies Kustomizations; {{c3::helm-controller}} reconciles HelmReleases; {{c4::notification-controller}} sends alerts and receives inbound webhooks.
notes.extra: Image update automation: image-reflector-controller + image-automation-controller.

notes.front: Which Flux source kinds exist?
notes.back: GitRepository, OCIRepository, HelmRepository (HTTP or Open Container Initiative (OCI)), HelmChart, Bucket (S3-compatible).

notes.front: Flux Kustomization custom resource (CR) vs Kustomize's kustomization.yaml?
notes.back:
Flux Kustomization (kustomize.toolkit.fluxcd.io): tells kustomize-controller which path from which source to build and apply, with interval, prune, health checks.
kustomization.yaml: the Kustomize build config itself (Flux generates one if absent).
notes.analogy: kustomization.yaml is the recipe; the Flux Kustomization is the kitchen order saying which recipe to cook, how often, and to clear away leftovers.

notes.front: Does a Flux HelmRelease create a real Helm release?
notes.back: Yes. helm-controller uses the Helm software development kit (SDK): the release shows in helm ls, hooks run natively, lookup works.
notes.extra: Contrast: Argo CD only runs helm template and applies the output.

notes.front: How does a Flux HelmRelease remediate failed installs/upgrades?
notes.back: install.remediation.retries / upgrade.remediation.retries with strategy: rollback or uninstall.

notes.front: What does HelmRelease driftDetection do?
notes.back: Compares the live cluster with the Helm release manifest; mode: enabled corrects drift, mode: warn only reports it.

notes.front: How do you order Flux reconciliations (e.g. custom resource definitions (CRDs) and infra before apps)?
notes.back: spec.dependsOn on Kustomizations/HelmReleases, combined with wait: true or healthChecks.

notes.text: Flux Kustomization fields: interval = {{c1::reconcile period}}; retryInterval = {{c2::retry period after a failure}}; prune = {{c3::garbage-collect objects removed from the source}}; wait = {{c4::block until all applied resources are ready}}.
notes.extra: timeout bounds apply + health checking.

notes.front: How does Flux decrypt SOPS-encrypted secrets?
notes.back: Natively in kustomize-controller: spec.decryption: {provider: sops, secretRef: {name: sops-age}} (age/PGP keys) or cloud key management service (KMS) via workload identity.

notes.front: What are Flux post-build variable substitutions?
notes.back: spec.postBuild.substitute / substituteFrom (ConfigMaps/Secrets) replace ${VAR} or ${VAR:=default} after the kustomize build.
notes.extra: Opt an object out with annotation kustomize.toolkit.fluxcd.io/substitute: disabled.

notes.front: What does flux bootstrap do?
notes.back: Installs the Flux controllers, commits their manifests plus a flux-system GitRepository + Kustomization to the repo, and sets up deploy keys — so Flux manages its own installation from Git.

notes.front: How does Flux enforce multi-tenancy?
notes.back: Per-object spec.serviceAccountName impersonation, controller flags --no-cross-namespace-refs and --default-service-account, and spec.targetNamespace.

notes.front: How can Flux deploy to a remote cluster?
notes.back: spec.kubeConfig.secretRef on a Kustomization/HelmRelease (or configMapRef for workload-identity auth), so a hub cluster applies to spokes.

notes.text: Flux image automation: {{c1::ImageRepository}} scans registry tags; {{c2::ImagePolicy}} selects the tag (semver/alphabetical/numerical); {{c3::ImageUpdateAutomation}} commits the new tag back to Git.
notes.extra: Manifests are marked with # {"$imagepolicy": "ns:policy"}.

notes.text: Flux notifications: a Provider is {{c1::a destination (Slack, Teams, GitHub commit status...)}}; an Alert {{c2::routes selected events to a provider}}; a Receiver is {{c3::an inbound webhook that triggers reconciliation}}.

notes.front: How do you force or pause a Flux reconciliation?
notes.back:
Force: flux reconcile kustomization x --with-source (sets reconcile.fluxcd.io/requestedAt).
Pause: flux suspend/resume or spec.suspend: true.

notes.front: How does Flux verify artifact authenticity?
notes.back: spec.verify on GitRepository (OpenPGP commit signatures) and OCIRepository (cosign or Notation signatures).

notes.front: What is the Flux-ecosystem equivalent of Argo Rollouts?
notes.back: Flagger: progressive delivery (canary, A/B, blue-green) with mesh/ingress traffic shifting and metric analysis.

notes.front: Argo CD vs Flux: architecture and UI?
notes.back:
Argo CD: application-centric server with built-in UI, single sign-on (SSO) and RBAC.
Flux: a set of composable controllers, no built-in UI, tenancy via Kubernetes RBAC + impersonation.
notes.extra: Both are CNCF-graduated; team familiarity and UI/SSO needs usually decide.

notes.front: Argo CD vs Flux: natural fleet topology?
notes.back:
Argo CD: hub-and-spoke — one instance manages many clusters.
Flux: per-cluster pull agents, each bootstrapped from a shared repo.

notes.front: Why does setting spec.serviceAccountName on a Flux Kustomization matter for multi-tenancy?
notes.back: Flux applies the manifests as that ServiceAccount, so a tenant is limited to what its role-based access control (RBAC) allows. Without it, kustomize-controller applies with its own (cluster-admin) rights, and a tenant could create anything.
notes.extra: Pair with --default-service-account so tenants cannot omit it.

notes.front: Declarative vs imperative Infrastructure as Code?
notes.back:
Declarative: describe the end state (Terraform, CloudFormation, Kubernetes manifests); the tool computes the diff.
Imperative: describe the steps (shell scripts, software development kit (SDK) scripts, many Ansible playbooks).
notes.analogy: Declarative gives the taxi driver the address; imperative gives turn-by-turn directions.

notes.front: What does idempotency mean in infrastructure as code (IaC), and why does it matter?
notes.back: Applying the same configuration N times gives the same result as applying it once. It makes retries, re-runs and continuous reconciliation safe.
notes.analogy: An elevator call button: pressing it five times still calls one elevator.
notes.extra: In Ansible: modules check current state and only act (report changed) when it differs from the desired state.

notes.front: What is configuration drift, and how is it detected?
notes.back: Divergence between declared state and real infrastructure, usually from manual/out-of-band changes. Detected by terraform plan (refresh) or continuously by reconcilers (Crossplane, Argo CD, Flux).

notes.front: Mutable vs immutable infrastructure?
notes.back:
Mutable: servers are patched in place → snowflakes and drift.
Immutable: never modify; build a new image and replace instances → reproducible, easy rollback.
notes.analogy: Pets vs cattle: pets are nursed back to health in place; cattle are replaced with an identical new one.

notes.front: Where is the line between Terraform and GitOps in a Kubernetes platform?
notes.back:
Terraform: cloud resources (networks, clusters, node pools, databases (DBs), DNS, identity and access management (IAM)) plus a one-time bootstrap of the GitOps agent.
GitOps (Argo/Flux + Helm): everything inside the clusters.

notes.front: Why not manage Kubernetes workloads with Terraform?
notes.back: No continuous reconciliation, state fights with in-cluster controllers, slow monolithic applies and plan noise — and kubeconfig credentials land in state. Terraform hands off; controllers keep the truth.

notes.text: Terraform core workflow: terraform init {{c1::downloads providers/modules and configures the backend}}; terraform plan {{c2::previews the diff between config and real infrastructure}}; terraform apply {{c3::executes that diff}}.

In Terraform, a resource is {{c1::an object Terraform creates, updates or deletes}}; a data source is {{c2::a read-only lookup}}; a module is {{c3::a reusable package of resources with inputs and outputs}}; a provider is {{c4::the plugin that turns resources into API calls for one platform}}.

notes.front: What is Terraform state, and why is it needed?
notes.back: A mapping from config resource addresses to real-world object IDs, plus cached attributes and dependency data. Needed to know what Terraform manages, compute diffs and order destroys.
notes.analogy: Terraform's inventory ledger: without it Terraform can't tell the objects it built from ones that merely look similar.

notes.front: Security concern with Terraform state?
notes.back: State stores attribute values in plaintext — including secrets, even ones marked sensitive. Use an encrypted remote backend with tight access control.
notes.extra: OpenTofu supports client-side state encryption.

notes.front: Why must remote Terraform state be locked?
notes.back: So two concurrent apply runs can't race and corrupt the state or make conflicting changes.
notes.analogy: A "room occupied" sign: only one apply may be inside editing the ledger at a time.

notes.front: How is Terraform state locked on the S3 backend (Terraform ≥ 1.10)?
notes.back: Native lockfile in the bucket (use_lockfile = true, relies on S3 conditional writes); the legacy way is a DynamoDB lock table.
notes.extra: azurerm: blob lease; gcs: lock object; HashiCorp Cloud Platform (HCP) Terraform: built in.

notes.front: count vs for_each: why prefer for_each for collections?
notes.back: count addresses by index (res[0]): removing a middle element shifts indices and destroys/recreates resources. for_each addresses by stable key (res["web"]).
notes.analogy: count is numbered seats — one person leaves and everyone shifts down; for_each is name tags.

notes.text: Terraform lifecycle: create_before_destroy {{c1::builds the replacement first, avoiding downtime}}; prevent_destroy {{c2::errors on any plan that would destroy the resource}}; ignore_changes {{c3::ignores drift on listed attributes}}; replace_triggered_by {{c4::forces replacement when a referenced item changes}}.

notes.front: How do you rename/move a resource in Terraform without destroying it?
notes.back: A moved { from = ... to = ... } block — declarative and reviewable in a PR.
notes.extra: Legacy: terraform state mv.

notes.front: How do you bring an existing resource under Terraform management?
notes.back: An import { to = aws_s3_bucket.b id = "name" } block, optionally with terraform plan -generate-config-out=gen.tf.
notes.extra: Legacy: CLI terraform import.

notes.front: Why is terraform apply -target dangerous?
notes.back: It applies a partial graph: dependent changes are skipped and state ends up inconsistent with the config. Only for exceptional recovery.
notes.analogy: Renovating one wall without checking the structural plan: the building record no longer matches the building.

notes.front: Purpose of .terraform.lock.hcl?
notes.back: Pins exact provider versions and checksums for reproducible init. Commit it.
notes.extra: Pitfall: it does not lock module versions.

notes.front: When do you need an explicit depends_on in Terraform?
notes.back: Only for hidden dependencies not expressed via references (e.g. an identity and access management (IAM) policy that must exist before an app uses it). Overuse makes plans less precise.

notes.front: What is terraform plan -refresh-only for?
notes.back: Shows drift and lets you accept it: updates state to match reality without proposing infrastructure changes.
notes.extra: Replaces the deprecated terraform refresh.

notes.front: Terraform CLI workspaces: what do they give you, and why do many teams avoid them for environments?
notes.back: Multiple state files for one configuration (terraform.workspace). All share one backend and credentials → weak isolation; teams prefer separate root modules per environment.

notes.front: Why does OpenTofu exist?
notes.back: HashiCorp moved Terraform to the Business Source License (BSL, restricts competing commercial use) in 2023; OpenTofu is the Linux Foundation fork that stays Mozilla Public License (MPL) 2.0 open source and largely drop-in compatible.
notes.extra: Adds features such as client-side state encryption.

notes.front: Pulumi vs Terraform in one line?
notes.back: Same desired-state engine idea, but infrastructure is written in general-purpose languages (TypeScript, Python, Go...) instead of HashiCorp Configuration Language (HCL).

notes.front: What does terraform plan compare, and what does it produce?
notes.back: It refreshes state against real infrastructure, then compares the configuration with that state. The output is the set of create / update / destroy actions needed to converge.

notes.front: You rename a resource block in Terraform without a moved block. What does the plan show, and why?
notes.back: Destroy the old address and create the new one. State maps resource addresses to real objects, so a new address looks like a brand-new resource.

notes.front: The Terraform state file is lost but the infrastructure still exists. What does the next plan propose, and how do you recover?
notes.back: It proposes creating everything again (Terraform believes nothing is managed), risking duplicates or conflicts. Recover by restoring state from backup or re-importing each resource.

notes.front: Provisioning vs configuration management?
notes.back:
Provisioning creates infrastructure (Terraform, CloudFormation).
Configuration management configures software on it (Ansible, Puppet, Chef).
notes.analogy: Provisioning builds the house; configuration management furnishes and maintains it.
notes.extra: Ansible is agentless and push-based; Puppet/Chef classically run agents that pull.

notes.front: What makes Ansible "agentless", and how does it reach targets?
notes.back: Nothing is installed on managed nodes: the control node pushes modules over SSH (Linux) or Windows Remote Management (WinRM) (Windows) and runs them there.

notes.text: Ansible architecture: the control node {{c1::runs Ansible}}; managed nodes are {{c2::the agentless targets}}; the inventory {{c3::lists hosts and groups}}; modules are {{c4::units of work executed on managed nodes}}.

Ansible structure: a play {{c1::maps a host group to an ordered list of tasks}}; a task {{c2::calls one module}}; a role {{c3::bundles tasks, handlers, variables and files for reuse}}; a playbook {{c4::contains plays}}.

notes.front: When does an Ansible handler run?
notes.back: Only when notified by a task that reported a change — once, at the end of the play (e.g. restart a service after its config changed).
notes.analogy: A "restart required" flag: any change can raise it, and it is acted on once at the end.

notes.front: Static vs dynamic inventory in Ansible?
notes.back:
Static: a fixed INI/YAML file of hosts.
Dynamic: generated at runtime by an inventory plugin querying a source (AWS EC2, Azure, Kubernetes...).

notes.front: What does Ansible Vault protect, and when is it decrypted?
notes.back: Sensitive variables/files (passwords, keys) encrypted at rest in the repo; decrypted only at runtime with the vault password/key.

notes.front: What is Ansible Galaxy?
notes.back: A public hub plus CLI (ansible-galaxy) for sharing and installing reusable roles and collections.

notes.text: A central Ansible controller (AWX and its downstream products) adds {{c1::a web UI/API with RBAC, scheduling and job history}} over the CLI, {{c2::execution environments}} (containerized, versioned Ansible runtimes) and {{c3::a curated content hub}} for approved roles and collections.
notes.extra: Example: Red Hat Ansible Automation Platform = Automation Controller (formerly Tower, AWX upstream) + Execution Environments + Automation Hub.

notes.front: Ansible module vs plugin: where does each run?
notes.back:
Module: runs on the managed node and does one unit of work (e.g. install a package).
Plugin: extends Ansible itself on the control node (inventory, connection, filter plugins).

notes.front: What are Ansible facts?
notes.back: System information (OS, IPs, hardware...) gathered from managed nodes by the setup module and usable as variables.

notes.front: Why is Ansible idempotency a property of the module and not of the playbook, and which modules break it?
notes.back: Idempotent modules check current state before acting. command and shell just run, so repeat runs repeat the effect unless you add creates or changed_when.

notes.front: A task runs shell: echo "line" >> /etc/app.conf. What goes wrong on the second run, and what is the fix?
notes.back: It appends the line again, since shell has no desired-state check. Use an idempotent module such as lineinfile, which only changes the file if the line is absent.

notes.front: What is Crossplane?
notes.back: A Kubernetes extension that turns a cluster into a control plane for external infrastructure: cloud resources become Custom Resources that providers reconcile continuously.

notes.front: How do Terraform and Crossplane differ in when they act on infrastructure?
notes.back:
Terraform: one-shot plan/apply runs triggered by a person or pipeline; drift is found only when a run happens.
Crossplane: controllers reconcile continuously, so drift is auto-corrected.
notes.analogy: Terraform is a contractor who visits when called; Crossplane is a building manager who lives on site and fixes things as soon as they change.

notes.front: What is a Crossplane Provider?
notes.back: A package that adds custom resource definitions (CRDs) + controllers for one external system (e.g. provider-aws), so Crossplane can manage that system's resources.

notes.front: What is a Crossplane Managed Resource (MR)?
notes.back: The lowest-level Crossplane resource: a Custom Resource that represents exactly one external resource (e.g. one S3 bucket).

notes.front: What is a Crossplane Composite Resource (XR)?
notes.back: A higher-level resource that bundles several managed resources (MRs) into one logical unit (e.g. a "Database" = network + instance + firewall rule).

notes.front: What does a Crossplane CompositeResourceDefinition (XRD) define?
notes.back: The schema of a Composite Resource — the platform API consumers see.

notes.front: What is a Crossplane Composition?
notes.back: The implementation behind a composite resource (XR)'s API: it defines which managed resources (MRs) an XR creates and how they are configured.
notes.analogy: The XRD is the interface, the Composition is the class implementing it — swap Compositions (AWS vs Azure) without changing the API.

notes.front: What is a Crossplane Claim?
notes.back: A namespaced request object through which app teams self-serve a Composite Resource without cluster-scoped permissions.
notes.extra: Crossplane v2 lets XRs themselves be namespaced, making Claims a legacy feature.

notes.front: What is a Crossplane Package?
notes.back: An Open Container Initiative (OCI) image used to install and version Providers, Configurations and Functions, pulled from any OCI registry.

notes.front: What are Crossplane Composition Functions?
notes.back: Pipeline steps inside a Composition that compute the composed resources with real code (Go, Python, Kusion Configuration Language (KCL)...) instead of patch-and-transform YAML templates.

notes.front: What is the "control plane abstraction" pattern behind Crossplane and KRO (Kube Resource Orchestrator)?
notes.back: Using the Kubernetes API server — declarative reconciliation, RBAC, custom resource definition (CRD) extensibility — as a universal control plane for any resource (cloud infra, SaaS, other K8s objects), not just workloads.
notes.analogy: The API server becomes the organisation's single order desk: every request, whatever it is for, goes through the same forms, permissions and follow-up process.

notes.front: Policy-as-code for infrastructure as code (IaC): which tool fits each job?
notes.back:
Conftest: Open Policy Agent (OPA) Rego against config or plan JSON in CI.
Sentinel: policy built into HashiCorp Cloud Platform (HCP) Terraform/Enterprise.
Checkov / Trivy (ex-tfsec): static misconfiguration scanners with built-in rules.

notes.front: Walk through how an app team's Crossplane Claim ends up as running cloud resources.
notes.back: The Claim creates a Composite Resource (XR), whose API is defined by the XRD. The Composition renders managed resources (MRs). Provider controllers call the cloud application programming interface (API), then keep reconciling.

notes.front: Why does Crossplane split the CompositeResourceDefinition (XRD) from the Composition?
notes.back: The XRD is the stable API app teams consume; the Composition is the swappable implementation. The platform can change how a Database is built (say, AWS to GCP) without touching any Claim.

notes.front: What does Crossplane do if someone deletes a managed cloud resource by hand?
notes.back: The provider controller observes the resource is missing versus the declared managed resource and recreates it, which is continuous drift correction. Terraform would notice only on its next plan.

notes.text: Helm terms: a chart is {{c1::a package of templates plus default values}}; a release is {{c2::an installed instance of a chart in a namespace}}; a revision is {{c3::a numbered version of a release (each upgrade or rollback adds one)}}; a repository {{c4::publishes charts (HTTP index or Open Container Initiative (OCI) registry)}}.
notes.analogy: Chart = recipe; release = a dish cooked from it in one kitchen (namespace); revision = each re-cook with changes.

notes.front: Why was Tiller removed in Helm 3?
notes.back: Tiller was an in-cluster server with broad privileges that bypassed per-user RBAC. Helm 3 is client-only and acts with the user's own kubeconfig permissions.
notes.extra: Helm 3 also brought three-way merge, namespace-scoped release names and apiVersion: v2 charts.

notes.front: Where does Helm 3 store release information, and what does it hold?
notes.back: As Secrets in the release namespace (type helm.sh/release.v1), holding the gzipped manifest, values and chart for each revision.
notes.extra: Secret name format: sh.helm.release.v1.<name>.v<rev>.

notes.front: Helm values precedence: which wins — chart values.yaml, -f files or --set?
notes.back: --set beats -f files, which beat the chart's values.yaml. Among several -f files the last (rightmost) wins.
notes.extra: Parent chart values override a subchart's own defaults.

notes.front: What does Helm 3's three-way merge compare on upgrade, and what is the effect?
notes.back: Old manifest, live state and new manifest. Manual live changes that conflict with the new chart are overwritten; unrelated live fields (e.g. injected sidecars) are preserved.
notes.analogy: An editor merging your redline into a document someone else also annotated: your changes win where they clash; untouched annotations survive.

notes.front: Helm: include vs template?
notes.back: Both render a named template. include returns a string so it can be piped ({{ include "x" . | nindent 4 }}); template is an action and can't be piped.

notes.front: What goes in a chart's _helpers.tpl?
notes.back: Named templates (define) such as fullname, labels, selectorLabels. Files starting with _ are not rendered as manifests.

notes.front: How does Helm treat custom resource definitions (CRDs) in the crds/ directory?
notes.back: Installed on first install only — never templated, upgraded or deleted. CRD upgrades must happen out of band (or ship CRDs as templates / a separate chart).

notes.front: Which three annotations control a Helm hook?
notes.back: helm.sh/hook (event, e.g. pre-upgrade), helm.sh/hook-weight (ordering), helm.sh/hook-delete-policy (before-hook-creation, hook-succeeded, hook-failed).

notes.front: Pitfall: are Helm hook resources managed as part of the release?
notes.back: No. They are not tracked as release resources, so uninstall/upgrade won't clean them up unless a hook-delete-policy does.

notes.front: How do you force pods to roll when a ConfigMap rendered by the same chart changes?
notes.back:
A checksum annotation on the pod template:
checksum/config: {{ include (print $.Template.BasePath "/configmap.yaml") . | sha256sum }}

notes.front: What does helm upgrade --install --atomic do?
notes.back: Installs if the release is absent, else upgrades; waits for readiness and automatically rolls back on failure (--atomic implies --wait).
notes.extra: Helm 4 renames --atomic to --rollback-on-failure.

notes.front: Does helm rollback restore the old revision number?
notes.back: No. It creates a new revision whose content equals the target revision.
notes.analogy: Like git revert: history moves forward with a new commit that restores old content.

notes.front: How are Helm chart dependencies declared and fetched?
notes.back: dependencies: in Chart.yaml (name, version, repository, optional condition/tags/alias); helm dependency update fetches them into charts/ and writes Chart.lock.

notes.front: How do a parent chart and its subcharts share values?
notes.back: The parent sets subchart values under the subchart's name key; .Values.global is visible to the parent and all subcharts.

notes.front: What is a Helm library chart?
notes.back: A chart with type: library that provides only named templates for reuse; it cannot be installed on its own.
notes.analogy: A header file: shared definitions you include, never run on their own.

notes.front: How do you validate Helm chart values?
notes.back: values.schema.json (JSON Schema), checked on install/upgrade/lint/template; inside templates, required and fail.

notes.front: Pitfall of the Helm lookup function?
notes.back: It queries the live cluster, so it returns an empty map under helm template, client-side dry-run — and in Argo CD, which renders with helm template.

notes.front: What does the Helm tpl function do?
notes.back: Renders a string as a template, enabling templated values: {{ tpl .Values.host . }}.

notes.front: How do you keep a resource when a Helm release is uninstalled?
notes.back: Annotation helm.sh/resource-policy: keep (common on persistent volume claims (PVCs) and Secrets); the resource is left orphaned.

notes.front: helm template vs helm install --dry-run?
notes.back: template renders locally with no cluster access (default capabilities, no lookup). install --dry-run contacts the cluster for validation but persists nothing.
notes.extra: --dry-run=server also enables lookup.

notes.front: How are Helm charts distributed via Open Container Initiative (OCI) registries?
notes.back: helm push chart.tgz oci://registry/ns and helm install x oci://registry/ns/chart --version 1.2.3 — no helm repo add needed.
notes.extra: General availability (GA) since Helm 3.8.

notes.front: What controls how many release revisions Helm keeps?
notes.back: --history-max on helm upgrade (default 10); older release Secrets are pruned.

notes.front: Headline changes in Helm 4?
notes.back: Server-side apply support, a WebAssembly-based plugin system and a modernised software development kit (SDK)/logging; Helm 3 charts (apiVersion: v2) still work.
notes.extra: Released November 2025.

notes.front: What is a Kubernetes Operator?
notes.back: A custom controller plus custom resource definitions (CRDs) that encodes human operational knowledge (install, upgrade, backup, failover) for one application in a reconciliation loop.
notes.analogy: A runbook turned into a robot SRE that watches the app around the clock and performs the steps itself.

notes.front: Level-triggered vs edge-triggered: which do Kubernetes controllers use, and why?
notes.back: Level-triggered: act on current observed vs desired state, not on individual events. A missed event is harmless because the next reconcile sees the full state.
notes.analogy: Edge-triggered answers the doorbell; level-triggered looks out of the window to see who is there — a missed ring doesn't matter.

notes.front: Why must Reconcile() be idempotent?
notes.back: It can run any number of times for the same object (resyncs, requeues, coalesced events) and must converge to the same result without duplicating side effects.

notes.front: Why does a controller receive only a namespace/name key, not the event diff?
notes.back: Level-triggered design: events are coalesced per key, and reconcile reads the current state from the cache.

notes.front: Custom resource spec vs status: who owns each?
notes.back: spec = desired state, written by the user. status = observed state, written by the controller.

notes.front: What does enabling the /status subresource change on a custom resource definition (CRD)?
notes.back: Status is written through a separate endpoint and spec updates ignore status — so RBAC can separate them, and generation bumps only on spec changes.

notes.front: metadata.generation vs resourceVersion?
notes.back:
generation: increments only on spec changes (with status subresource).
resourceVersion: opaque, changes on every write; used for optimistic concurrency and watches.
notes.analogy: generation is the edition number of the order form (changes only when the order changes); resourceVersion is a timestamp stamped on every touch, even a sticky note.

notes.front: What is status.observedGeneration for?
notes.back: The controller records the generation it last reconciled, so clients can tell whether status reflects the latest spec.

notes.front: How does an Operator use finalizers to clean up external resources?
notes.back: A finalizer string blocks deletion: deleting sets deletionTimestamp, the controller does external cleanup (e.g. deletes the cloud database (DB)), then removes its finalizer so the object goes away.
notes.analogy: A "do not discard until signed off" sticker: the object can't be thrown away until the controller removes its sticker after cleanup.

notes.front: What do OwnerReferences enable, and what are their limits?
notes.back: The garbage collector deletes dependents when their owner is deleted. Owner must be in the same namespace (or cluster-scoped); for cross-namespace or external resources use finalizers.
notes.analogy: Delete the parent folder and the garbage collector clears out everything filed inside it.

notes.text: Cascading deletion: background (default) {{c1::deletes the owner immediately, and garbage collection (GC) removes dependents afterwards}}; foreground {{c2::deletes dependents first}}; orphan {{c3::keeps dependents and strips their ownerReferences}}.

notes.front: How do multiple Operator replicas avoid conflicting with each other?
notes.back: Leader election via a coordination.k8s.io Lease: only the leader runs the controllers.
notes.analogy: A talking stick: only the Lease holder reconciles; the others grab it if the holder disappears.

notes.front: How should a controller handle a 409 Conflict on update?
notes.back: It's optimistic concurrency on resourceVersion: re-fetch and retry, or use server-side apply / patches instead of full-object updates.

notes.front: Why is Server-Side Apply (SSA) useful for controllers?
notes.back: The API server merges declared fields and tracks ownership per field manager (managedFields), so a controller sends only the fields it owns and conflicts become explicit.

notes.front: Custom resource definition (CRD) versioning: served vs storage version?
notes.back: Many versions can be served; exactly one is the storage version. Non-trivial schema differences need a conversion webhook.

notes.front: Which Custom Resource validation option supports cross-field rules without running a webhook?
notes.back: Common Expression Language (CEL) rules in the custom resource definition (CRD) schema (x-kubernetes-validations), evaluated in the API server.
notes.extra: Other options: OpenAPI v3 schema; ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (cluster-wide CEL); validating/mutating admission webhooks.

notes.text: Operator tooling: controller-runtime is {{c1::the Go library (manager, client, cache)}}; Kubebuilder {{c2::adds scaffolding and code generation on top of it}}; Operator SDK {{c3::builds on Kubebuilder and adds Helm/Ansible operators plus Operator Lifecycle Manager (OLM) bundle tooling}}.

Operator capability levels: 1 Basic Install → 2 Seamless Upgrades → 3 Full Lifecycle = {{c1::backup/restore and failure recovery}} → 4 Deep Insights = {{c2::metrics and alerts}} → 5 Auto Pilot = {{c3::auto-scaling, tuning and self-healing}}.

notes.front: What does the Operator Lifecycle Manager (OLM) do?
notes.back: Installs and upgrades Operators with their dependencies and RBAC, via CatalogSources, Subscriptions, InstallPlans and ClusterServiceVersions (CSVs). Default on OpenShift.

notes.front: Fields of a conventional status condition?
notes.back: type, status (True/False/Unknown), reason (CamelCase), message, lastTransitionTime, observedGeneration.

notes.front: Why shouldn't a controller write status on every reconcile unconditionally?
notes.back: Each write bumps resourceVersion → new watch event → another reconcile: a hot loop that loads the API server. Compare before writing.
notes.extra: controller-runtime's GenerationChangedPredicate also filters out status-only update events.

notes.front: Describe one pass of an Operator's reconcile loop and why it is safe to run again.
notes.back: Read the custom resource spec from the cache, observe actual state, compute the difference, make only the missing changes, write status, requeue if needed. Idempotent steps make reruns harmless.

notes.front: What breaks if an Operator creates an external cloud database but does not use a finalizer?
notes.back: Deleting the custom resource removes it at once, so the controller never sees the deletion. The cloud database is orphaned, still running and billing.

notes.front: A controller crashes after creating 1 of 3 child resources. Why is that recoverable without special handling?
notes.back: Reconcile is level-triggered and idempotent. The next pass observes the current state, finds the 1 existing child, and creates only the 2 missing ones.

notes.front: What breaks if two replicas of an Operator run without leader election?
notes.back: Both reconcile the same objects at once, causing conflicting writes (409 Conflict errors) and duplicate external resources. A Lease lets only the leader run controllers.

notes.front: What breaks if a controller creates a child Deployment but sets no ownerReference on it?
notes.back: Deleting the custom resource leaves the Deployment orphaned (no garbage collection). Watches on owned children also cannot map child events back to the parent.

notes.deck: Platform Engineering::09 Platform as a Product
notes.front: What does treating a platform as a product mean?
notes.back: The platform team works like a product team: app teams are internal customers, and the roadmap is driven by discovery, feedback and adoption metrics rather than top-down mandate.

notes.deck: Platform Engineering::09 Platform as a Product
notes.front: What does a platform team own, and how is its success measured?
notes.back: It owns the Internal Developer Platform as a product (not business features). Success = developer adoption, lead time and satisfaction — not story points delivered.

notes.deck: Platform Engineering::09 Platform as a Product
notes.front: What is the Thinnest Viable Platform (TVP)?
notes.back: The smallest platform that solves developers' most painful problems, grown iteratively from real usage instead of built all-encompassing up front.
notes.analogy: A minimum viable product for internal customers: ship the smallest thing that removes the biggest pain, then grow it.
notes.extra: Can be as small as a wiki page of documented standards and services.

notes.deck: Platform Engineering::09 Platform as a Product
notes.front: What does a platform product manager do?
notes.back: Runs discovery with developers as customers, prioritises the roadmap (e.g. which golden path next) and tracks adoption, DevOps Research and Assessment (DORA) metrics and developer satisfaction.

notes.deck: Platform Engineering::09 Platform as a Product
notes.front: What does "X-as-a-Service" mean in platform engineering?
notes.back: Capabilities (database (DB) provisioning, CI templates, observability setup) exposed as self-service APIs/UI that developers consume directly instead of filing tickets.

notes.deck: Platform Engineering::09 Platform as a Product
notes.front: Main risk of building a platform without a product mindset?
notes.back: Low adoption: developers route around a mandated but unloved platform (shadow IT), undermining the standardisation it was built for.

notes.deck: Platform Engineering::09 Platform as a Product
notes.front: Define golden path in platform engineering.
notes.back: An opinionated, documented, platform-supported way to build, deploy and run a service for a common use case — the easiest path, not the only allowed one.
notes.analogy: A paved path through a park: most people walk on it because it's easiest, but the grass isn't fenced off.

notes.deck: Platform Engineering::09 Platform as a Product
notes.front: Golden path vs golden cage?
notes.back: A golden path stays optional with supported escape hatches. It becomes a golden cage when it is the only allowed path — killing autonomy and creating bottlenecks and resentment.

notes.deck: Platform Engineering::09 Platform as a Product
notes.front: How do golden paths reconcile standardisation with team autonomy?
notes.back: By making the compliant path the path of least resistance instead of a mandate.

notes.deck: Platform Engineering::09 Platform as a Product
notes.front: What does a typical "new microservice" golden path bundle?
notes.back: Repo scaffold, wired CI/CD pipeline, baseline observability/logging, security scanning, standard base image and deployment manifest — delivered as one self-service template.

notes.deck: Platform Engineering::09 Platform as a Product
notes.front: Which signals show a golden path is failing?
notes.back: Low opt-in, teams building unofficial parallel pipelines, frequent exception requests, and platform engineers having to intervene manually.

notes.deck: Platform Engineering::09 Platform as a Product
notes.front: Your platform team mandated a golden path and adoption is low. What does a product mindset say to do first?
notes.back: Interview the developers who route around it to find the friction, then fix the biggest pain. Adoption comes from being the easiest path, not from mandates.

notes.deck: Platform Engineering::10 Developer Portals & Workload Specs
notes.front: What is Backstage?
notes.back: A Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) open-source framework (from Spotify) for building an internal developer portal: one UI for the software catalog, docs, CI/CD status and scaffolding templates.

notes.deck: Platform Engineering::10 Developer Portals & Workload Specs
notes.front: Internal Developer Platform vs Internal Developer Portal?
notes.back:
Platform: the underlying tools, APIs and infrastructure that provide self-service.
Portal: the UI layer (often Backstage) through which developers discover and use it.
notes.analogy: The platform is the kitchen; the portal is the menu and ordering counter.

notes.deck: Platform Engineering::10 Developer Portals & Workload Specs
notes.front: What is the Backstage Software Catalog?
notes.back: The system of record for the software estate: YAML entities tracking ownership, relationships and lifecycle of services, APIs, libraries and resources.
notes.analogy: A phone book plus org chart for software: who owns what, and what depends on what.

notes.deck: Platform Engineering::10 Developer Portals & Workload Specs
notes.front: What is a Backstage entity descriptor made of?
notes.back: A YAML document with apiVersion, kind, metadata and spec, describing one real thing (service, API, team...).

notes.deck: Platform Engineering::10 Developer Portals & Workload Specs
notes.text: Backstage entity kinds: a Component is {{c1::a piece of software (service, website, library)}}; an API is {{c2::an interface that components provide or consume}}; a Resource is {{c3::infrastructure a component needs (database, bucket)}}.
notes.extra: Other kinds: System, Domain, Group, User, Location, Template.

notes.deck: Platform Engineering::10 Developer Portals & Workload Specs
notes.front: Backstage: System vs Domain?
notes.back: A System groups Components/APIs/Resources that together deliver one capability (e.g. payments). A Domain groups related Systems into a business area (e.g. finance).

notes.deck: Platform Engineering::10 Developer Portals & Workload Specs
notes.front: Why does a Backstage Component's spec.owner matter so much?
notes.back: It resolves to a Group/User (synced from GitHub teams, Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP), Okta) and drives "who do I ask" and on-call/alert routing — a stale owner is worse than none.

notes.deck: Platform Engineering::10 Developer Portals & Workload Specs
notes.front: What is catalog-info.yaml, and where should it live?
notes.back: The per-repo descriptor for that repo's catalog entities; keep it next to the source code so ownership metadata stays current.

notes.deck: Platform Engineering::10 Developer Portals & Workload Specs
notes.front: How does Backstage keep the catalog populated automatically?
notes.back: Entity providers scan sources (GitHub orgs, S3...) on a schedule and ingest YAML definitions; processors validate and enrich each entity.

notes.deck: Platform Engineering::10 Developer Portals & Workload Specs
notes.front: What is TechDocs, and how is it linked to an entity?
notes.back: A Backstage plugin rendering Markdown docs kept with the code inside the entity page, wired via the backstage.io/techdocs-ref annotation.

notes.deck: Platform Engineering::10 Developer Portals & Workload Specs
notes.front: What does Backstage's Scaffolder do, and which entity kind defines its templates?
notes.back: It generates new projects from parameterised software templates (kind Template): a form wizard plus steps that create a repo with the golden path pre-wired.

notes.deck: Platform Engineering::10 Developer Portals & Workload Specs
notes.front: Why do organisations adopt a packaged Backstage distribution instead of building on vanilla Backstage?
notes.back: Vanilla Backstage is a framework: RBAC, audit logging, plugin curation, upgrades and support are do-it-yourself. A distribution ships that hardening pre-built, at the cost of less control over the stack.
notes.extra: Examples: Red Hat Developer Hub, Roadie, Spotify Portal.

notes.deck: Platform Engineering::10 Developer Portals & Workload Specs
notes.front: Backstage plugins: statically compiled vs dynamic loading?
notes.back: Static: plugins are compiled into the app bundle; adding one means rebuild and redeploy. Dynamic: plugins are loaded at startup from configuration, so a plugin can be enabled without rebuilding the app.
notes.extra: Example: Red Hat Developer Hub enables dynamic plugins via dynamic-plugins.yaml.

notes.deck: Platform Engineering::10 Developer Portals & Workload Specs
notes.front: What is Score?
notes.back: A Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) Sandbox, platform-agnostic workload specification: a developer describes a workload's runtime needs once in score.yaml, independent of the target platform.
notes.analogy: A universal plug spec: the workload declares the plug it needs, and each environment supplies a matching socket.

notes.deck: Platform Engineering::10 Developer Portals & Workload Specs
notes.front: What problem does Score mainly solve?
notes.back: Config drift between environments (e.g. Docker Compose locally vs a Helm chart remotely): one source of truth that each Score implementation translates per target.

notes.deck: Platform Engineering::10 Developer Portals & Workload Specs
notes.text: Score reference implementations: {{c1::score-compose}} targets Docker Compose (local dev); {{c2::score-k8s}} generates Kubernetes manifests.

notes.deck: Platform Engineering::10 Developer Portals & Workload Specs
notes.front: What is a Score resource provisioner?
notes.back: A pluggable translator from an abstract dependency in score.yaml ("a postgres database") to a concrete one per environment — a local container locally, a Terraform-provisioned instance in prod.

notes.deck: Platform Engineering::10 Developer Portals & Workload Specs
notes.text: Platform orchestrator pattern: at deploy time it reads the abstract workload spec → matches {{c1::each declared dependency to an environment-specific resource definition}} → creates or updates those resources → deploys the workload with the generated configuration.
notes.extra: Example: Humanitec calls this RMCD (Read, Match, Create, Deploy); Score is the open workload spec it consumes.

notes.deck: Platform Engineering::10 Developer Portals & Workload Specs
notes.front: What is dynamic configuration management, as opposed to static per-environment config files?
notes.back: A workload's environment-specific configuration (endpoints, credentials, resource bindings) is assembled on demand at deploy time from the workload spec plus environment rules, instead of being hand-maintained per environment.
notes.extra: Example: Humanitec markets this as "DCM"; it is what a platform orchestrator does between workload spec and deployment.

notes.deck: Platform Engineering::10 Developer Portals & Workload Specs
notes.front: Where does a platform orchestrator sit relative to the developer portal and the deployment tooling?
notes.back: As a backend layer between them: the portal (e.g. Backstage) is the interface, the orchestrator resolves workload specs into concrete resources and manifests, and existing tools (Argo CD, Terraform) still provision and deploy. It complements them rather than replacing them.
notes.extra: Examples: Humanitec Platform Orchestrator, Kratix.

notes.deck: Platform Engineering::10 Developer Portals & Workload Specs
notes.front: How do Score and a Backstage Scaffolder template complement each other?
notes.back: Score defines what a workload needs to run; the template defines how a new project is created. The template can emit a score.yaml as one of its outputs.

notes.deck: Platform Engineering::10 Developer Portals & Workload Specs
notes.front: How do Backstage Software Catalog, Scaffolder and TechDocs depend on one another?
notes.back: A Scaffolder template creates a repo containing catalog-info.yaml, which registers it in the catalog. That file's TechDocs annotation links docs in the repo to the entity page.

notes.deck: Platform Engineering::10 Developer Portals & Workload Specs
notes.front: In Score, how does a workload ask for a database without naming a specific one?
notes.back: It declares an abstract resource (e.g. type: postgres) in score.yaml. A per-environment provisioner resolves it to a local container or a cloud instance.

notes.deck: Platform Engineering::10 Developer Portals & Workload Specs
notes.front: Describe what a platform orchestrator does at deploy time, step by step.
notes.back: Read the abstract workload spec; match each declared dependency to an environment-specific resource definition; create or update those resources; deploy the workload with the generated configuration.

notes.front: What is Kyverno?
notes.back: A Kubernetes-native policy engine running as an admission controller; policies are Kubernetes YAML resources, not a separate language like Rego.

notes.text: Kyverno rule types: validate {{c1::accepts or rejects resources}}; mutate {{c2::patches resources before they are persisted}}; generate {{c3::creates companion resources (e.g. a default NetworkPolicy per namespace)}}.
notes.analogy: validate is the bouncer, mutate the tailor adjusting your outfit at the door, generate the concierge handing out a welcome pack.
notes.extra: Plus verifyImages for signature/attestation checks.

notes.front: What does Kyverno's background scanning do?
notes.back: Periodically re-evaluates policies against resources already in the cluster, surfacing violations that predate the policy.

notes.front: What is Kyverno's verifyImages rule for?
notes.back: Verifying image signatures (Cosign/Sigstore) and attestations at admission, rejecting unsigned or tampered images.

notes.front: What is Kyverno auto-gen for Pod controllers?
notes.back: A rule written against Pods is automatically expanded to Deployments, StatefulSets, Jobs etc., so you don't duplicate rules per controller kind.

notes.front: How do Kyverno and Gatekeeper hook into the Kubernetes admission chain?
notes.back: They register Validating/MutatingWebhookConfigurations, so the API server calls them on each matching request.

notes.front: Policy webhooks (Kyverno/Gatekeeper) vs ValidatingAdmissionPolicy: key difference?
notes.back: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy runs Common Expression Language (CEL) expressions inside the API server — no webhook to operate or time out. Webhook engines add mutation, generation, image verification and richer logic.
notes.extra: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy is general availability (GA) since Kubernetes 1.30.

notes.front: What is Open Policy Agent (OPA)?
notes.back: A general-purpose policy engine: policies in Rego (a declarative query language) evaluated over any JSON input — not Kubernetes-specific.

notes.front: What does Gatekeeper add on top of Open Policy Agent (OPA) to make it usable as a Kubernetes admission control?
notes.back: Gatekeeper wraps OPA as a Kubernetes validating (and mutating) admission controller and adds custom resource definitions (CRDs) (ConstraintTemplate, Constraint) on top of raw Rego.

notes.text: Gatekeeper: a ConstraintTemplate {{c1::defines reusable Rego logic plus a parameter schema}}; a Constraint {{c2::instantiates it with concrete parameters and a match scope}}.
notes.analogy: ConstraintTemplate is the class, Constraint is an object created from it.

notes.front: What does Gatekeeper's Config sync do?
notes.back: Replicates chosen cluster resources into Open Policy Agent (OPA)'s cache so Rego can reference other objects (e.g. all Namespaces), not just the incoming request.

notes.front: What does Gatekeeper audit do?
notes.back: Periodically evaluates existing resources against active Constraints and records violations in their status (like Kyverno background scans).

notes.front: Kyverno vs Open Policy Agent (OPA)/Gatekeeper: when to choose which?
notes.back:
Kyverno: YAML, Kubernetes-native, fastest for common K8s policies.
OPA/Gatekeeper: Rego is more expressive and reusable beyond K8s (CI, APIs, Terraform), better for complex cross-resource logic.

notes.front: What happens to API requests if the admission webhook of a policy engine is unreachable, for failurePolicy: Fail versus Ignore?
notes.back:
Fail: matching requests are rejected, so a webhook outage can block cluster operations.
Ignore: requests are admitted unchecked, so policy is silently bypassed.

notes.front: A new policy is installed, yet old non-compliant resources exist. Why did admission not catch them, and what does?
notes.back: Admission only evaluates requests as they are created or updated. Kyverno background scans and Gatekeeper audit re-evaluate existing resources and report violations.

notes.front: Why do mutating admission steps run before validating ones?
notes.back: Mutation can change the object, so validation must see the final version. Otherwise it could approve an object that later mutation changes into a violation.

notes.front: What is Sigstore?
notes.back: Open-source infrastructure for signing, verifying and recording provenance of artifacts (images, binaries, software bills of materials (SBOMs)) without long-lived private keys.

notes.front: What is Cosign?
notes.back: Sigstore's client for signing and verifying Open Container Initiative (OCI) container images and other OCI artifacts.

notes.front: What is Sigstore keyless signing?
notes.back: Signing with a short-lived certificate from Fulcio bound to an OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity (e.g. a GitHub Actions workflow), instead of a long-lived key the signer must guard.
notes.analogy: Like a visitor badge issued at reception after an ID check and valid for minutes; the reception logbook (Rekor) proves you held it when you signed.

notes.front: What is Fulcio?
notes.back: Sigstore's certificate authority: issues minutes-long X.509 signing certificates bound to a verified OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity.

notes.front: What is Rekor?
notes.back: Sigstore's transparency log: an append-only, verifiable ledger of signing events, so anyone can audit when and by whom an artifact was signed.
notes.analogy: A public notary's logbook: entries can't be erased, so anyone can check when something was signed and by whom.

notes.front: Why is Rekor needed when Fulcio certificates expire after minutes?
notes.back: Verifying later requires proof the signature was made while the cert was valid; Rekor's timestamped log entry provides that proof.

notes.front: Where does Cosign store an image signature?
notes.back: As a separate Open Container Initiative (OCI) artifact in the same registry, tagged from the image digest — the image manifest itself is unchanged.

notes.front: Cosign attestation vs plain signature?
notes.back: A signature asserts "signed by X". An attestation (cosign attest) is a signed in-toto statement carrying structured data about the artifact, e.g. a software bill of materials (SBOM) or Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts (SLSA) provenance.

notes.front: What is a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM)?
notes.back: A machine-readable inventory of the components and dependencies in a piece of software, with versions and ideally licenses.
notes.analogy: The ingredients label on food packaging: when a recall (CVE) hits, you can check instantly whether you're affected.

notes.front: What are the two dominant software bill of materials (SBOM) formats?
notes.back: Software Package Data Exchange (SPDX) (Linux Foundation, license-compliance roots, ISO standard) and CycloneDX (Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP), security roots).

notes.text: Anchore tools: {{c1::Syft}} generates a software bill of materials (SBOM) from an image, filesystem or archive; {{c2::Grype}} matches SBOM components against vulnerability databases to report Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs).

notes.front: How is a software bill of materials (SBOM) attached to an image for later verification?
notes.back: As a Cosign attestation (cosign attest --predicate sbom.json), signed and stored next to the image so consumers can verify authenticity and content.

notes.front: What is SLSA, and what problem does it address?
notes.back: Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts: incremental requirements for hardening build/release pipelines against tampering, centred on verifiable provenance.

notes.front: What is Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts (SLSA) provenance?
notes.back: A signed in-toto attestation describing how an artifact was built: source repo/commit, builder identity, build steps and inputs.
notes.analogy: A certificate of origin for software: where, from what, and by whom it was built.

notes.front: What is a hermetic build?
notes.back: A build with no undeclared external inputs or network access, so every dependency is explicit and the output is reproducible from stated inputs.
notes.analogy: Cooking in a sealed kitchen with only the listed ingredients, so the dish can be reproduced exactly.

notes.front: What does each rising Build Level of Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts (SLSA) v1.0 protect against that the previous level did not?
notes.back:
L1: provenance exists (but could be forged or missing).
L2: a hosted build platform signs the provenance, so tampering is detectable.
L3: hardened, isolated builds whose signing material build steps cannot reach, so provenance cannot be forged.

notes.front: Which format do Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts (SLSA) provenance, software bill of materials (SBOM) attestations and scan results share?
notes.back: The in-toto attestation format (subject + predicate envelope), so all can be signed and verified the same way.

notes.text: Supply-chain flow: the build emits an artifact plus Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts (SLSA) provenance → Cosign signs it and attests provenance and the software bill of materials (SBOM), logged in {{c1::Rekor}} → at admission, a {{c2::Kyverno verifyImages}} rule (or Gatekeeper policy) checks signature and attestations before admitting the Pod.

notes.front: Which capability areas does a Kubernetes security platform typically bundle?
notes.back: Vulnerability management (image/CVE scanning), configuration and compliance checks (Center for Internet Security (CIS), Pod Security), network segmentation visibility, and runtime threat detection — one view across build, deploy and run.
notes.extra: Examples: StackRox (open source; basis of Red Hat Advanced Cluster Security), Sysdig, Wiz, Aqua.

notes.front: How does an image scanner act as a CI/CD gate?
notes.back: A CLI or plugin step scans the freshly built image for vulnerabilities and policy violations and exits non-zero on a violation, failing the build before the image reaches the registry or cluster.
notes.extra: Examples: trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL, grype --fail-on high, roxctl image check (ACS).

notes.front: How does an observed-traffic network graph help with NetworkPolicies?
notes.back: It shows which pods actually talk to which (allowed and denied flows), so you can generate a least-privilege policy from real communication patterns and validate a proposed policy before enforcing it.
notes.extra: Examples: Cilium Hubble service map, Red Hat Advanced Cluster Security (ACS) network graph, Kubescape network-policy generation.

notes.front: Full-lifecycle Kubernetes security platform vs admission policy engine (Kyverno/Gatekeeper): how do their scopes differ?
notes.back: A security platform spans build-time scanning, deploy-time admission (its own webhook) and runtime detection. Kyverno/Gatekeeper focus on admission-time policy. Both complement the Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts (SLSA)→Cosign→verify chain.
notes.extra: Example: StackRox / Red Hat Advanced Cluster Security (ACS).

notes.front: Trace an image from build to admission: what is produced, signed, logged and checked?
notes.back: The build emits the image plus provenance and the software bill of materials (SBOM). Cosign signs and attests them, with Rekor logging it. At admission, a policy verifies signature and attestations.

notes.front: A container image is signed. Why is the signature alone not enough to trust it?
notes.back: A signature only proves who signed. It says nothing about how the image was built or what it contains, so you also need provenance and SBOM attestations, and a check of the signer's identity.

notes.front: What attack do hermetic builds plus provenance block that signing alone does not?
notes.back: A compromised build that pulls tampered inputs from the network: signing would faithfully sign the bad output. Hermetic builds forbid undeclared inputs, and provenance records the inputs.

notes.front: In Sigstore keyless verification, what must a verifier check besides a valid signature?
notes.back: That the certificate identity (issuer and subject, e.g. a specific continuous integration (CI) workflow) matches what you expect. Otherwise anyone with any valid identity could sign.

notes.text: Kubernetes multi-tenancy: {{c1::soft}} tenancy separates trusted tenants (internal teams) against accidents and noisy neighbours; {{c2::hard}} tenancy isolates mutually untrusted tenants against deliberate escape attempts.
notes.analogy: Soft tenancy is roommates locking doors against accidents; hard tenancy is separate apartments built to stop burglars.

notes.front: Which question decides whether you need soft or hard multi-tenancy?
notes.back: "What is the worst credible actor inside a tenant, and what must they never reach?"
notes.extra: Compliance zoning (classification levels, prod vs non-prod) often forces hard boundaries regardless of trust.

notes.text: Namespace-per-tenant combines: {{c1::RBAC}} scoped to tenant namespaces; {{c2::ResourceQuota}} caps; {{c3::LimitRange}} defaults so quotas are enforceable; {{c4::NetworkPolicy}} default-deny between tenants; {{c5::admission policy}} (Pod Security, no hostPath/privileged); {{c6::PriorityClass / tainted node pools}} to protect system workloads.

Namespace isolation still shares: the {{c1::control plane}} (one API server + etcd — noisy tenants degrade all); {{c2::cluster-scoped resources}} (custom resource definitions (CRDs), webhooks, ClusterRoles — operator versions collide); {{c3::node kernels}} (a container escape lands next to other tenants); and {{c4::one Kubernetes version and upgrade window}}.
notes.analogy: Namespaces are office cubicles: your own desk, but shared air conditioning, lifts and one building maintenance schedule.

notes.front: What is vCluster?
notes.back: A virtual cluster: a real kube-apiserver + datastore running as pods inside a host namespace; a syncer schedules its pods onto the host's nodes.
notes.analogy: Apartments in one building: each tenant gets its own front door and keys (API server), but they share foundations and plumbing (nodes, kernel, network).

notes.front: What does vCluster give tenants that namespaces don't?
notes.back: Their own API server: own custom resource definitions (CRDs), webhooks and versions without collisions, cluster-admin rights, fast and cheap creation (no cloud control-plane fee).

notes.front: What does vCluster not isolate?
notes.back: Nodes/kernels (workloads share host nodes), network beyond host NetworkPolicy, and host-cluster outages.

notes.front: Where is vCluster's sweet spot?
notes.back: Many dev/test tenants, self-service and ephemeral CI clusters on top of a few well-governed host clusters.

notes.text: Namespace-as-a-service tools: {{c1::Capsule}} groups namespaces into a Tenant custom resource definition (CRD) so tenant owners self-create namespaces within guardrails; {{c2::Hierarchical Namespace Controller (HNC)}} gives parent/child namespaces with policy propagation.
notes.extra: Value: tenancy becomes self-service, with quotas, NetworkPolicies and RBAC templates propagated automatically.

notes.front: Tenancy model for trusted internal teams with standard workloads?
notes.back: Namespaces + quotas + NetworkPolicy on a shared cluster — cheapest and densest.

notes.front: Tenancy model for teams that need their own custom resource definitions (CRDs), operators or cluster-admin?
notes.back: vCluster on shared host clusters.

notes.front: Tenancy model when one tenant has elevated data sensitivity and the rest are standard?
notes.back: Shared cluster plus a dedicated tainted node pool for that tenant, with stricter policies.

notes.front: Tenancy model for untrusted tenants or regulatory separation (prod/compliance zones)?
notes.back: Cluster-per-tenant (or per zone), in separate cloud projects/accounts.

notes.front: Shared ingress controller vs per-tenant ingress controllers?
notes.back:
Shared (+ IngressClass, hostname policy, rate limits): cheap, one load balancer.
Per-tenant: config blast-radius isolation and independent tuning, at N× LB cost.

notes.front: Multi-tenant monitoring: why prefer per-tenant agents feeding a multi-tenant backend over one shared Prometheus?
notes.back: In a shared Prometheus one tenant's cardinality explosion hurts everyone; per-tenant agents shipping to Mimir/Thanos (or per-tenant instances) scale and isolate cleanly.

notes.front: Which tenant limits are usually forgotten next to CPU/memory quotas?
notes.back: Metric cardinality, log volume and ingress config size — set explicit limits for them too.

notes.text: Reasons to run multiple clusters: {{c1::environment separation}} with independent upgrade cadence; {{c2::tenant/compliance isolation}}; {{c3::blast-radius control}} (bad rollout, poisoned custom resource definition (CRD), control-plane outage stays local); {{c4::upgrade canarying}} in rings; {{c5::placement}} (on-prem + cloud).
notes.extra: Anti-reason: "one cluster per microservice" — cluster count must track automation maturity.

notes.front: Management (hub) cluster + workload clusters: what runs where?
notes.back:
Hub: small, hardened; runs fleet machinery (Argo CD/Flux, secrets tooling, backup orchestration, observability aggregation).
Workload clusters: golden stack + tenant apps, all reconciled from Git.

notes.front: Why should the management (hub) cluster host zero tenants?
notes.back: It holds credentials to every cluster — it's the crown jewel; any tenant workload there widens the attack surface on the whole fleet.
notes.analogy: Don't open a café inside the bank vault.

notes.front: Fleet GitOps with a central (push) Argo CD: main drawbacks?
notes.back: The hub must reach every kube-apiserver, stores credentials for all clusters (crown-jewel target), and a hub outage stalls the whole fleet.

notes.front: Fleet GitOps with per-cluster pull agents: strengths and costs?
notes.back:
+ outbound-only from clusters, keeps reconciling through hub/WAN outages, scales horizontally.
− N installs to upgrade, fleet visibility needs aggregation, per-cluster bootstrap.

notes.front: Why do hybrid (on-prem + cloud) fleets lean toward pull-based GitOps?
notes.back: The wide area network (WAN) link is the least reliable component; pull agents keep reconciling the last known state when it fails.

notes.front: How do you layer Helm values so 30 clusters don't become 30 snowflakes?
notes.back: One golden-stack repo with a narrowing values hierarchy: global.yaml → env/prod.yaml → cluster/<name>.yaml (last wins). Cluster files stay tiny — mostly names and IPs.

notes.front: Fleet config: when Helm, when Kustomize, and why use umbrella charts sparingly?
notes.back: Helm for parameterised third-party software; Kustomize overlays for your own manifests. Umbrella charts couple component versions together.

notes.front: Fleet config rule: how must every per-cluster divergence be expressed?
notes.back: As a values/overlay line with a reviewable diff in Git — never a manual edit on the cluster; bots (e.g. Renovate) pin chart versions per ring.

notes.front: Default multi-cluster networking recommendation, and the rule for anything beyond it?
notes.back: Independent clusters + DNS/GSLB: cross-cluster calls go through normal ingress/LBs. Add cross-cluster networking only for a named requirement.

notes.front: Cilium ClusterMesh: what does it need, and why is it risky on managed Kubernetes?
notes.back: Pod-to-pod routing across clusters; needs non-overlapping pod Classless Inter-Domain Routing blocks (CIDRs), mutual reachability and control of the Container Network Interface (CNI) — which a managed service usually doesn't give you.

notes.front: Istio multi-cluster: benefit and cost?
notes.back: mTLS and locality failover across clusters via east-west gateways, without Container Network Interface (CNI) coupling — but operationally heavy.

notes.front: Submariner vs Skupper for connecting clusters?
notes.back:
Submariner: L3 tunnels between cluster networks (CNI-adjacent constraints).
Skupper: L7 application interconnect with no network coupling — good for selectively sharing a few services.

notes.front: Why is data gravity the real constraint in multi-cluster design?
notes.back: Stateless workloads move freely; data doesn't — block volumes are zone/cluster-local and databases replicate on their own terms.
notes.analogy: Stateless apps travel like suitcases; databases are the heavy furniture that needs a moving truck and a plan.

notes.text: Answers to data gravity, in order of preference: {{c1::externalise state to managed services}} reachable from any cluster → {{c2::application-level replication}} between sites → {{c3::backup/restore}} as the fallback.
notes.extra: Anti-pattern: stretching etcd, storage or synchronous replication across a wide area network (WAN)/VPN.

notes.front: How do you roll changes out across a fleet safely?
notes.back: Upgrade rings: lab → dev → staging → prod-canary → prod-rest; promote Git changes ring by ring with soak time and automated verification.
notes.analogy: A restaurant chain trying a new dish in one branch, then a region, before every branch.
notes.extra: PodDisruptionBudgets + surge-capable node pools keep drains safe; Renovate turns version bumps into per-ring diffs.

notes.front: Why does a ResourceQuota on CPU and memory reject pods that omit resource requests, and how does a LimitRange help?
notes.back: When a quota covers CPU or memory, every pod must state requests/limits, or it is rejected. A LimitRange injects default values, so tenants' pods are admitted and still counted.

notes.front: Why do the rollout rings go lab, dev, staging, prod-canary, then the rest of prod?
notes.back: Each ring has more realism and a larger blast radius than the last. A bad change is caught where it hurts least, and soak time plus automated checks gate each promotion.

notes.front: When a central hub Argo CD goes down, what happens to workloads on the managed clusters?
notes.back: They keep running, but nothing is reconciled or deployed fleet-wide until the hub returns. Per-cluster pull agents avoid this single point of failure.

notes.front: When you add a new workload cluster to a GitOps fleet, what does Terraform do and what does GitOps do?
notes.back: Terraform creates the cluster and bootstraps the GitOps agent, or registers the cluster with the hub. Labelling the cluster then lets ApplicationSets or Flux roll the golden stack onto it.
